title: Three Questions Leaders Must Answer Before Delegating a Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article distinguishes between high-stakes, irreversible decisions and the far more numerous two-way decisions that can be changed later with minimal disruption. Because leaders can't personally shepherd every two-way decision, the author argues the real skill is delegation, guided by three questions: who is the right person to decide, who else should be involved, and who else should have input. Once those questions are answered, the piece argues, leaders should hand over authority and resist the urge to keep advising. It closes by tying good delegation directly to developing future decision-makers.
points: Two-way decisions are important but reversible, and make up most of what leaders decide day to day
Leaders can't personally manage the quality of every two-way decision, so delegation is essential
Three questions precede good delegation: who decides, who else is involved, who else has input
Letting others make decisions and observe the results is how future leaders develop judgment
quotes: These are generally referred to as two-way decisions, meaning they are important but can be reversed and changed without significant disruption or discomfort to the team or organization.
Pushing down decisions to others is not only expedient but also necessary for developing other leaders.
To assist them with decision delegation, the best leaders ask and answer three foundational questions regarding any two-way decision they do not want to control.
With that limited guidance, the delegated decision-maker is set up for success.
More than half the battle of making a quality decision comes down to who is making it and who else is weighing in.
